artifactEvidence.excerpt: OpenAI released its Agents API in public beta on September 10. It gives developers a managed way to build software that keeps a task’s history, uses connected tools and resumes later. An API is a connection one piece of software uses to call another. This is not a new button in ChatGPT.

A model produces each response. A harness is the surrounding software that keeps the task history, tools, coordination and recovery organized. OpenAI manages that harness; an app maker supplies the tools and decides where the work runs.

A longer task can still finish badly. OpenAI’s documentation says a completed turn does not guarantee every tool succeeded. A “completed” label means the turn ended; it is not evidence that each file, search, message or booking inside the task succeeded.

readerValue.reason: Beyond the headline, the reader gains three usable boundaries: completed ≠ succeeded, no-fee ≠ free, and environment location ≠ retention policy.

explainBack.question: Why can an app built on this service truthfully report a task as 'completed' even though the message it was supposed to send never went out?
explainBack.answer: Because 'completed' is a status the managed harness assigns when a turn of work ends, while the actual sending happens through a separate tool the app maker supplied. The model's response and the harness's bookkeeping can finish cleanly even if an individual tool call — the one that sends the message — failed along the way. OpenAI's own documentation says a completed turn does not guarantee every tool succeeded, so the label records that the work cycle ended, not that each external action inside it landed.
explainBack.expectedEvidence: The answer must distinguish turn completion (harness status) from individual tool success, identify tools as app-maker-supplied and separately fallible, and cite the documented caveat rather than asserting general unreliability.
explainBack.assessment: The article supports this fully: P004 gives the model/harness/tool split, P006 quotes the caveat and interprets the label correctly, so an attentive reader can reconstruct the causal chain in ordinary language.

unseenTransfer.scenario: Months from now, a small-business bookkeeping app advertises that its assistant, built on a managed agent service, can 'reconcile the month': it pulls bank transactions, matches receipts, files the VAT summary with the tax portal, and emails the accountant. After twenty minutes it shows 'Reconciliation complete ✓'.
unseenTransfer.question: Using this article's mechanism, what should the owner check before assuming the VAT filing and the accountant email actually happened, and what should she ask about the app beforehand?
unseenTransfer.answer: Apply the access/completion/record triad. Access: check which services the app is connected to — bank feed, tax portal, email — since the app maker chose those tools and filing versus emailing are separate capabilities that can fail independently. Completion: treat the checkmark as meaning only that the work cycle ended; the harness status does not prove the tax-portal submission tool or the email tool succeeded. Record: open the tax portal for a submission receipt with a reference number and check the sent-mail record, rather than trusting the in-app summary. Beforehand, she should also read the app's terms on retained session data, since the service keeps session state regardless of where the app's own tools run.
unseenTransfer.expectedEvidence: A correct answer separates harness completion status from per-tool outcomes, names independent confirmation records for each consequential action, and applies the retention-versus-environment distinction to a new domain.
unseenTransfer.assessment: The article's mechanism transfers cleanly: P004/P006 supply the completion-versus-tool logic, P008 the retention distinction, and P009–P010 the verification triad, all applicable without stretching to this unseen bookkeeping case.
